title: Barry Melrose Was Hockey’s Mulleted, Larger-Than-Life Ambassador
subtitle: As a coach, and then especially across decades as a broadcaster, Melrose brought Canada’s game to American audiences, combining wit and wisdom in a tough-but-warm package.
contentHtml:
Barry Melrose was born in Kelvington, Saskatchewan, a small prairie town whose population stands at just 864 today — and was smaller still in the 1950s and ‘60s, when one of its most famous residents grew up on a farm nearby. But Melrose, the former NHL player, coach and longtime broadcaster who died at age 70 on Wednesday, would ultimately go on to gain fame well beyond the Canadian hinterlands.

One could argue, in fact, that he was on the short-list of ambassadors who helped popularize hockey in America, becoming one of the sport’s most iconic national-TV personalities at exactly the moment it was finally breaking through on U.S. airwaves.

Subscribe now

Life for American-based hockey fans has never been easy, between the sport’s dearth of coverage compared with, say, basketball, and the constant carousel of networks carrying games. But things were far worse leading up to the mid-1990s, when the NHL had gone nearly two decades without a regular, over-the-air national television partner in the United States. Following the expiration of NBC’s contract in 1975, the league wandered through the U.S. broadcasting wilderness — relying on a patchwork of regional networks and scattered cable coverage instead, which in turn kept the sport mostly out of the mainstream American consciousness.

Melrose’s playing career happened to overlap that period entirely. Taken in Round 2 of the 1976 entry draft, he logged 478 career WHA/NHL games as a stay-at-home defenseman from 1976-1986. Not long thereafter, he transitioned to coaching, winning both the Memorial Cup and Calder Cup — the top prizes in Canadian major-junior hockey and the American Hockey League, respectively — in his first five seasons after retiring as a player. So impressive a coaching commodity was Melrose that he was tasked with coaching Wayne Gretzky and the Los Angeles Kings at the age of just 351 in 1992.

Talk about a high-profile (and high-pressure) gig — one which didn’t get off to a great start. With the Great One sidelined half the year after a back injury, L.A. ranked sixth out of eight Campbell Conference playoff teams in points. But in the playoffs, Gretzky returned to lead the league in scoring, and the Kings pulled off a string of upsets to reach the Stanley Cup Final. While L.A. fell to the Montreal Canadiens in 5 games, Melrose was a hit with American fans thanks to his trademark mullet haircut and no-nonsense, motivational Canadian manner, with just a hint of humor underneath.

The next few years saw L.A. struggle to reclaim their ‘93 form, resulting in Melrose’s dismissal as coach in May 1995. But the Kings’ loss was a gain for both ESPN and hockey fans across America, as the network hired Melrose to be a studio analyst on the nightly NHL 2Night program while building out its still-growing coverage team. Melrose would go on to be a fixture at the network for most of the next three decades, becoming one of the most prominent faces of the sport in the process.

We can quantify just how much of a TV-hockey mainstay Melrose was by concocting a simple scoring system for broadcasters on major U.S. network and cable-channel NHL coverage. For each year of service, we’ll assign points based on the prominence of both platform and role:

  • Platform: 2 points for broadcast networks (such as ABC, NBC and Fox); 1.5 for major cable channels (such as ESPN, TNT and NBCSN); 1 for secondary or specialty channels (such as ESPN2, Versus and NHL Network, plus ESPN+ streaming).

  • Role: 4 points for the lead play-by-play announcer or primary game analyst; 3 for a lead studio host/analyst (this was Melrose’s job); 2 for secondary game commentators or between-the-benches analysts; 1 for other studio contributors/reporters.

Assigning those for each NHL season since 1994-95 — the importance of which I’ll explain below — we get the following array of significant NHL announcers in the U.S.:

Melrose was one of the faces of NHL TV coverage in the U.S.

Some broadcasters had enormous prominence for a shorter period, such as ESPN’s Gary Thorne — arguably the most iconic hockey announcer of this era, but who somehow only did it for a little over 10 years — while others were long-running mainstays in slightly less prominent roles, such as the diminutive goalie-turned-analyst Darren Pang. At the top of both categories, we have the longtime NBC duo of Mike “Doc” Emrick — generally regarded as the greatest modern voice of hockey — and his color-commentary partner Eddie Olczyk.

But the closest name to them on the chart2 is Melrose, who was sometimes a booth commentator but usually a studio analyst instead at ESPN, whether the network had NHL rights or not. (As Dan Patrick pointed out in his remembrance of Melrose, his former colleague kept the fire for hockey burning at the “Mothership” even after losing the broadcast deal in 2005, and nobody was more excited for the NHL on ESPN’s return in 2021.)

From his TV debut in 1995 through his retirement in 2023 — notwithstanding a very brief hiatus to coach the Tampa Bay Lightning in 2008 — Melrose did the thing he was put on this planet to do. Part old-school coach, part hockey evangelist and always the consummate showman, Melrose made hockey feel cool and accessible for an American audience — all facilitated through his combination of loud suits, that magnificent mullet, and a gravelly Saskatchewan delivery that simultaneously conveyed toughness, warmth and a slightly mischievous sense of humor.3

And Melrose’s tenure happened to coincide perfectly with hockey’s rapid growth in the States. Sports Illustrated ran its famous “Why The NHL’s Hot / And The NBA’s Not” cover on June 20, 1994, roughly 10 months before Melrose would join the TV ranks. A few months after that, FOX would embark on Year 1 of a landmark national-television deal that brought network coverage of NHL games for the first time in roughly 20 years.

The “FOX Attitude” of hockey-robots (see above) and glowing pucks set the tone for a new era in the NHL, seeking to appeal to younger fans and/or those in nontraditional regions. Melrose bridged that gap better than anyone — because of his knowledge of the game, enthusiasm for teaching it to new fans, and natural instinct for turning hockey’s seemingly impenetrable quirks into entertainment value. The timing for having an ambassador like that could hardly have been any better.

Melrose came along at exactly the right moment to grow the game

Hockey’s breakthrough south of the Canadian border was never the work of just one person, of course. Our own chart above is littered with Melrose’s contemporaries — many of whom worked alongside him, and who issued heartfelt statements upon the news of his death.

But few embodied that project as much as Melrose did. He arrived on the national-TV scene just as his sport was trying to convince a new generation of Americans to add the NHL to a growing stable of sports that would make up the ESPN-loving fan’s lifestyle. For the next 30 or so years, he’d make hockey’s sales pitch with an authenticity and charisma that was hard to deny — something that would ultimately become the biggest part of his own legacy, too.
